question_text: A 57-year-old female presents with dyspnea on exertion. Pulmonary function studies with plethysmography demonstrate an increase in the work of breathing, and the oxygen consumption is higher-than-normal at rest. Which of the following will decrease the oxygen consumption of the respiratory muscles?
option_c: A decrease in the diffusing capacity of the lung
option_d: An increase in the rate of respiration
explanation:
Respiratory muscles consume oxygen in proportion to the work of breathing. The work of breathing is equal to the product of the change in volume for each breath and the change in pressure necessary to overcome the resistive work of breathing and the elastic work of breathing.

Resistive work includes work to overcome tissue as well as airway resistance; thus a decreased airway resistance will decrease the work of breathing and the oxygen consumption of the respiratory muscles.

A decreased lung compliance would increase the elastic work of breathing. An increase in respiratory rate or tidal volume increases the work of breathing.

question_text: A hospitalized patient has tachypnea and significantly labored respirations requiring mechanical ventilation. Based on the pressure-volume curve of the lungs shown as Curve Z in the figure below, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for the patient?
explanation:
Lung compliance is defined as the ease with which the lungs are expanded, and is calculated as the change in volume per change in pressure (ΔV/ΔP), which is the slope of the pressure-volume curve of the lung.

Thus, Curve Z is the pressurevolume curve of an individual with a decrease in lung compliance. The abnormal accumulation of fluid in the lungs (pulmonary edema) causes a restrictive pulmonary impairment characterized by a decreased lung compliance.

An L/S ratio $2 indicates normal biochemical maturation of the lung, with normal surfactant production and lung compliance (normal curve).

If the L/S ratio is less than 2, there is an increased incidence of respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn, which would be represented by Curve Z. Aging and emphysema are characterized by an increase in lung compliance (Curve X), which increases airway resistance.

The increase in airway resistance in asthma is not associated with an increase (or decrease) in lung compliance.

Reference: Ganong, pp 654-658. Levitzky, pp 20-28.

It is calculated using Bohr's equation, which compares arterial and expired CO₂ concentrations.

Key Takeaways:

  • Physiological dead space = anatomical + alveolar dead space.
  • Reflects ventilation-perfusion mismatch due to poor perfusion.
  • Cannot be measured by spirometry.

question_text: Type 2 pneumocytes produces lung surfactants. The surfactants reduce the surface tension in the alveoli. A defect in type 2 pneumocytes or surfactant deficiency can lead to:
explanation:
A defect in type 2 pneumocytes or surfactant deficiency can lead to respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).

  • Role of Surfactant: Surfactant reduces surface tension in the alveoli, preventing collapse.
  • Condition: In hyaline membrane disease (commonly seen in premature infants), surfactant production is greatly decreased, leading to increased surface tension and alveolar collapse.
  • Timing: Surfactant production begins around 20-24 weeks of gestation but reaches sufficient levels usually after 35 weeks.
  • Treatment: Antenatal corticosteroids can be administered to increase surfactant production in at-risk mothers.

Why Not Others:

  • Pneumonia: Involves infection and inflammation of lung tissue, not specifically related to surfactant deficiency.
  • Bronchiectasis: Characterized by abnormal widening of the bronchi and is not primarily due to surfactant issues.
  • Emphysema: Involves destruction of alveolar walls and is primarily caused by smoking or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, not surfactant deficiency.

Key takeaways:

  • A defect in type 2 pneumocytes or surfactant deficiency leads to respiratory distress syndrome, characterized by high surface tension in the alveoli, often seen in premature newborns.

question_text: The diagram below illustrates the intrapleural pressure generated by a patient during a forced expiration. The equal pressure point will move closer to the mouth and the forced expiratory volume will increase if there is an increase in which of the following?
explanation:
The equal pressure point is the point at which the pressure inside the airways equals the intrapleural pressure. The intra-airway pressure closest to the alveoli equals the sum of the recoil pressure (exerted by the alveoli) and the intrapleural pressure (produced by the muscles of expiration).

The equal pressure point moves further away from the lungs if the recoil force is increased and moves closer to the lungs when the intrapleural pressure is increased. Increasing the lung volume expands the alveoli, making their recoil force greater and the intrapleural pressure less (more negative).

This moves the equal pressure point toward the mouth. If airway resistance increases by increasing airway smooth muscle tone or increasing lung compliance, then a greater expiratory effort and consequently a greater intrapleural pressure will be necessary to expel the gas from the lungs.

The higher intrapleural pressure when airway resistance is increased will cause the equal pressure point to be reached closer to the alveoli, decreasing the volume of gas exhaled, and increasing residual volume due to air trapping behind the compressed airways.

Reference: Levitzky, pp 37-40.

question_text: A 6 feet 3 inches tall, 140-lb, 20-year-old male was watching television when he felt pain in his shoulder blades, shortness of breath, and fatigue. option_b: The chest wall on the affected side recoils inward

explanation:
When air enters the pleural space due to interruption of the pleural surface through either the rupture of the lung or a hole in the chest wall, the pressure in the pleural space becomes atmospheric, the lung on the affected side collapses because of the lung's tendency to recoil inward, and the chest wall on the affected side recoils outward.

question_text: A preterm infant born at 28 weeks develops signs of respiratory distress syndrome. Which statement accurately describes the changes in surface tension and lung compliance in this condition?
option_c: Both surface tension and compliance decreased
option_d: Both surface tension and compliance increased
explanation:
Explanation:

Surface tension increased and compliance decreased; this statement is accurate regarding surface tension and compliance in a preterm baby with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).

Elastic tissue recoil and surface tension are the two opposing forces to lung compliance, and are not opposing forces to each other.

Two primary factors influence lung compliance:

  • Elastic forces of the lung tissue:
    • These forces are primarily determined by the presence of elastin and collagen fibres within the lung parenchyma (the functional tissue of the lungs).
    • In a deflated lung, these fibres are contracted and kinked. As the lung expands during inspiration, these fibres stretch and unkink, generating an elastic force that opposes further expansion.
  • Surface tension:
    • A thin layer of fluid lines the inside of the alveoli. At the air-fluid interface within the alveoli, surface tension arises from the stronger attraction between water molecules compared to the attraction between water molecules and air molecules.
    • This surface tension creates an inward pull, attempting to minimise the surface area of the fluid lining the alveoli. Consequently, this inward pull contributes to the elastic recoil of the lungs, making them tend to collapse.

Reference: Pulmonary Compliance - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question_text: Which of the following occurs during normal quiet expiration?
explanation:
Explanation:

Normal quiet expiration is a passive process. It occurs mainly due to:

  • Elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall
  • Relaxation of the diaphragm

There is no active muscular contraction involved in quiet expiration.

During quiet expiration:

  • Diaphragm relaxes and moves upward (Option C)
  • Thoracic cavity decreases in volume (Option A)
  • Elastic tissues of lung recoil back inward
  • Intrapulmonary pressure rises slightly, pushing air out

No active contraction of intercostal or abdominal muscles occurs.

During Deep Inspiration:

  • Movements during quiet inspiration are increased
  • The first rib is elevated by scaleni
  • The concavity of thoracic spine is reduced by erector spinae.

During Forced Inspiration:

  • All above movements are exaggerated.
  • The scapulae are elevated and fixed by trapezius, levator scapulae so that serratus anterior and pectoralis minor may act on the ribs
  • The action of erector spinae is also increased

During Deep and forced expiration:

  • Strong contraction of abdominal muscles and of latissimus dorsi.

Concavity of spine reduced (Option D): Quiet expiration does not significantly involve spinal movement.

Key takeaway:

Respiratory movements range from increasing thoracic diameters during inspiration to relying on elastic recoil and abdominal muscle contraction during expiration, with variations in intensity depending on the type of breathing.

question_text: A preterm neonate develops respiratory distress soon after birth. The pediatrician suspects neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) due to inadequate surfactant secretion. Which type of pulmonary cell is primarily responsible for surfactant production in the lungs?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Type 2 pneumocytes are cuboidal cells located in the alveoli.
  • They synthesize and secrete pulmonary surfactant, composed mainly of dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC), phospholipids, and surfactant proteins (SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D).
  • Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis), and enhances lung compliance.
  • Surfactant secretion begins around 20-24 weeks gestation and becomes adequate after 34-36 weeks, which explains why preterm neonates are at high risk of RDS.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Type 1 pneumocyte (Option A): Flat squamous cells covering ~95% of alveolar surface; specialized for gas exchange, not surfactant secretion.

Alveolar macrophage (Option B): Immune phagocytic cells that clear pathogens and debris; no role in surfactant production.

Dust cells (Option C): Another name for alveolar macrophages → immune defense role only, not surfactant secretion.

Key Takeaway points:

Clinical Correlation:

  • Neonatal RDS: Caused by surfactant deficiency → alveolar collapse, hypoxemia, "ground-glass" appearance on CXR. Treated with exogenous surfactant & maternal steroids (Betamethasone) if preterm delivery anticipated.
  • ARDS (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome): Secondary surfactant dysfunction due to alveolar damage (sepsis, trauma, aspiration, etc.).

question_text: A patient with right lower lobar pneumonia exhibits increasing respiratory distress. The patient is intubated, placed on a mechanical ventilator, and positioned on his left side. The dependent lung has a lower:
option_a: Rate of alveolar ventilation per unit volume
explanation:
Even in normal individuals, the dependent lung has a greater ventilation per unit volume and a greater pulmonary blood flow, but because the effects of gravity (hydrostatic pressure) are greater for blood than air because blood is more dense, the increase in perfusion exceeds the increase in ventilation, and the V/Q ratio decreases.

An area with a lower V/Q has less gas exchange, and thus Paco2 increases and PaO2 decreases. These changes are exacerbated in pneumonia, which causes an increase in the number of low V/Q areas in the lung.

The greater hydrostatic pressure in the dependent lung causes an increased (less negative) intrapleural pressure, which decreases lung volume, and places the pressure-volume curve of the lung on a steeper slope (increased compliance).

In patients with unilateral pneumonia, simply positioning the unaffected lung downward may result in improved ventilation-perfusion matching and an increase in PaO2 of 10-15 mmHg.

Reference: Ganong, pp 662-663. Kasper et al., p 1537. Levitzky, pp 125-127.

question_text: A 28-year-old on oral contraceptives develops tachypnea and reports dyspnea. A ventilation/perfusion scan is ordered to check for pulmonary thromboemboli. Which of the following best explains why, as she takes in a normal inspiration, more air goes to the alveoli at the base of the lung than to the alveoli at the apex of the lung?
option_a: The alveoli at the base of the lung have more surfactant
option_b: The alveoli at the base of the lung are more compliant
option_c: The alveoli at the base of the lung have higher V/Q ratios
option_d: There is a more negative intrapleural pressure at the base of the lung
explanation:
During inspiration, when all alveoli are subjected to essentially the same alveolar pressure, more air will go to the more compliant alveoli in the base of the lung.

Because the lungs are essentially "hanging" in the chest, the force of gravity on the lungs causes the intrapleural pressure to increase (become less negative) at the base of the lungs compared to the apex (more negative intrapleural pressure).

This also causes the alveoli at the apex of the lung to be larger than those at the base of the lung.

Larger alveoli are already more inflated and are less compliant than smaller alveoli. Because of the effect of gravity on blood, more blood flow will go to the base of the lung.

Ventilation is about three times greater at the base of the lung, but flow is about 10 times greater at the base than at the apex of the lung; therefore, the V/Q ratio is lower at the base than at the apex in a normal lung.

Reference: Ganong, pp 658. Levitzky, pp 125-127.

question_text: An 18-year-old girl presents to her primary care physician with an increased frequency of asthma exacerbations over the previous year. At the time of her visit, her physical examination and flow-volume loop are normal. At which point on the flow-volume loop pictured below will airflow remain constant despite an increased respiratory effort?
explanation:
A maximal expiratory flow volume curve is generated during a forced vital capacity maneuver. Only the initial expiratory flow is effort-dependent.

That is, increasing expiratory effort will increase expiratory flow at points E and A (peak flow), but not at point B, which is referred to as the effort-independent portion of the maximal expiratory flow-volume curve.

The inability to increase flow rates during the efffort-independent portion is caused by compression of the noncartilaginous airways by the positive intrapleural pressures that are generated during a forced expiration when the expiratory muscles are actively contracted, a phenomenon called dynamic compression of the airways.

No effort limitation occurs during inspiration (points C and D) because increased inspiratory efforts make the intrapleural pressure more negative, which expands the airways, lowering their resistance.

Reference: Levitzky, pp 44-48.

question_text:
A 68-year-old woman convalescing from surgery developed a fever, hypoxemia, and shortness of breath. She was given 100% O2 for 30 minutes, and the lab results were as follows:
PaO2 = 95 mmHg
PaCO2 = 33 mmHg
pH = 7.46 [HCO3 -] = 22 mEq/L [Hb] = 15 g%
SaO2 = 95%
The response to 100% O2 reveals that the patient has which of the following?
option_c: V/Q inequality with low V/Q units
explanation:
The classification of the causes of hypoxemia (low PaO2) are

  1. Reduced PAO2 (alveolar hypoventilation or reduced PIo2 found at high altitude or with breathing low concentrations of oxygen),
  2. Diffusion impairment,
  3. Ventilation/perfusion inequality, and
  4. Right-to-left shunting (venous admixture).

Left-to-right shunting does not cause hypoxemia.

Administration of 100% O2 corrects the hypoxemia caused by alveolar hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, or ventilation/perfusion inequality, but not that due to right-to-left shunting (venous admixture). Alveolar hypoventilation would have an increased PaCO2. In carbon monoxide poisoning, the SaO2 would be lower than normal.

On 100% O2, the PaO2 should be 1500 mmHg and the A-a PO2 difference should be "100 mmHg". This patient's Pao2 is only 95 mmHg on 100% O2, indicating the presence of right-to-left shunting, that is, areas of the lung that are perfused but not ventilated (V/Q ratio = 0). Post-op complications such as pneumonia, pulmonary edema, and atelectasis are all causes of intrapulmonary right-to-left shunts.

Reference: Ganong, pp 683-691. Levitzky, pp 180-183.

question_text: A medical student waiting to do her first patient interview at the Clinical Skills Center becomes very anxious and increases her rate of alveolar ventilation. If her rate of CO2 production remains constant, which of the following will decrease?
explanation:
Because the deadspace air does not participate in gas exchange, the entire output of CO2 in the expired gas comes from the alveolar gas.

Accordingly, CO2 output (VCO2) can be expressed in terms of alveolar ventilation (VA) and alveolar PCO2, according to the equation: PaCO2 = VCO2 /VA Because PaCO2 is essentially equal to PaCO2, this equation can also be expressed as PaCO2 = VCO2/VA. Thus, an increase in alveolar ventilation at a constant rate of carbon dioxide production will lower the PaCO2 and PaCO2.

Hyperventilation increases PaO2 and PaO2, with no change in the alveolar-arterial PaO2 difference.

The V/Q would be normal or increased.

question_text: A 36-year-old man with a history of AIDS and Pneumocystis infection presents to the Emergency Department with severe respiratory distress. The patient is placed on a ventilator at a rate of 16, tidal volume of 600 mL, and FIO2 of 1.0. An arterial blood sample taken 20 minutes later reveals a Po2 of 350 mmHg, a Pco2 of 36 mmHg, and a pH of 7.32. At a barometric pressure of 757 mmHg, and assuming a normal respiratory exchange ratio (R) of 0.8, the patient's alveolar oxygen tension is approximately which of the following?
explanation:
The alveolar air equation is used to calculate the PAO2.

PAO2 = PIO2 - (PaCO2/R) Given the barometric pressure of 757 mmHg, FIO2 = 1.0 (100% O2), PaCO2 = 36 mmHg, and R = 0.8, then PAO2 = (1.0)(757 - 47) - (36/0.8) = 710 - 45 = 665 mmHg

Pneumocystis is an opportunistic fungal pulmonary pathogen that is an important cause of pneumonia (pneumocystosis) in immunocompromised hosts. HIV patients with a CD4 + cell count below 200/μL have an increased risk of developing Pneumocystis pneumonia.

According to new, and still evolving nomenclature, Pneumocystis carinii is the name of the organism derived from rats, and Pneumocystis jiroveci is the name of the organism derived from humans.

question_text: In a Pattern baby with respiratory distress syndrome, which type of cell is deficient?
explanation:
Type 2 alveolar cells are responsible for producing surfactant, a substance that reduces surface tension in the lungs, preventing alveolar collapse and facilitating normal lung function. Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in newborns, especially in preterm infants, is due to the immature or insufficient production of surfactant. This leads to alveolar collapse, impaired gas exchange, and respiratory distress.

Incorrect Options:

  • Type 1 alveolar cell: These cells cover the majority of the alveolar surface and are involved in gas exchange. They are not responsible for surfactant production, which is the primary issue in RDS.
  • Alveolar capillary endothelial cells: These cells form the blood-air barrier and are important for gas exchange, but surfactant deficiency is not related to their function in RDS.
  • Bronchial mucosal epithelial cells: These cells line the bronchi and bronchioles and are involved in mucus production and airway protection. They are not the source of surfactant and are not deficient in RDS.

Key Takeaways:

  • Type 2 alveolar cells produce surfactant, which is deficient in respiratory distress syndrome.
  • RDS is common in preterm infants, where immature lungs cannot produce enough surfactant, leading to alveolar collapse and breathing difficulties.
  • Treatment options include surfactant replacement therapy and respiratory support.

question_text: A 56-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe abdominal pain and a temperature of 103°F. The patient is in severe respiratory distress. His alveolar oxygen tension, at a barometric pressure of 747 mmHg and a respiratory exchange ratio (R) of 0.8, is approximately what?
explanation:
The alveolar oxygen tension is calculated using the modified alveolar gas equation:

PAO2 = PIO2 - PaCO2/R.

PAO2 = [0.5 x (747 - 47 mmHg)] - 40 mmHg/0.8

PAO2 = 350 mmHg - 50 mmHg = 300 mmHg

question_text: A 68-year-old man who has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents to his pulmonologist with fatigue, dyspnea at rest, and peripheral edema. His blood gases on room air are PaO2 = 60 mmHg, PaCO2 = 60 mmHg, and pH = 7.36. His alveolar-arterial (A-a) O2 gradient, at a barometric pressure of 760 mmHg and a respiratory exchange ratio (R) of 0.8, is approximately what?
explanation:
The A-a O2 gradient is the partial pressure difference between the alveolar gas and arterial blood. The PaO2 has been measured. The alveolar oxygen tension must be calculated using the modified alveolar gas equation

PAO2 = PIO2 - PaCO2/R

PAO2 = [0.21 x (760 - 47 mmHg)] - 60 mmHg/0.8

PAO2 = 150 mmHg - 75 mmHg = 75 mmHg

(A-a) O2 gradient = 75 mmHg - 60 mmHg = 15 mmHg

The patient's low arterial oxygen tension (hypoxemia; hypoxic hypoxia) results from a low PAO2 due to hypoventilation (as evidenced by the elevated PaCO2), and thus the (A-a) O2 gradient is within the normal range.

Reference: Levitzky, pp 75, 180-181, 262.

question_text: A hospitalized patient is found semicomatose. Arterial blood gases reveal hypercapnia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the high arterial PCO2?
explanation:
Profound hypoxia depresses the central nervous system, including the medullary respiratory centers.

As a result, alveolar ventilation may decrease, resulting in an increased PaCO2. A decrease in metabolic activity would decrease the rate of production of carbon dioxide (VCO2), which would decrease PaCO2, assuming that alveolar ventilation does not change.

If an alveolar capillary block is severe, retention of CO2 could briefly occur, but the coexistent hypoxemia would cause reflex hyperventilation with a decrease in PaCO2.

At a constant tidal volume and respiratory rate, a decrease in the deadspace volume would increase alveolar ventilation, and thus lower the PaCO2.

question_text: A 24-year-old woman collapsed in a New York City subway station. An autopsy showed that a blood clot had travelled to her lung and caused her death. question_text: The given graph shows PCo2 and PO2 of the right lung along with ventilation and perfusion ratio. Which point on the graph represents V/Q ratio if there is a complete block of the blood supply at alveolar level of right lung due to pulmonary embolism?
explanation:
Explanation:

The provided graph is an O2-CO2 diagram illustrating how the V/Q ratio determines alveolar gas composition. Pulmonary embolism creates alveolar dead space (V/Q = ∞), where alveolar gas mirrors inspired air (Point E).

Normal Ventilation-Perfusion (V/Q) Ratio:

  • Average: 0.8 (ventilation = 4.2 L/min, perfusion = 5.4 L/min).
  • Apex of lung: V/Q ~ 3 (high ventilation, low perfusion).
  • Base of lung: V/Q ~ 0.6 (high perfusion, low relative ventilation).

Pulmonary Embolism Physiology:

  • Definition: Complete blockage of pulmonary artery → no blood flow (Q = 0) to ventilated alveoli.
  • Effect: Alveoli still receive air (V > 0) → alveolar dead space.
  • V/Q ratio: V/Q = V/0 = ∞ → maximal V/Q.
  • Alveolar gases:
    • PO2 ≈ PiO2 ≈ 150 mmHg (same as inspired air).
    • PCO2 ≈ 0 mmHg (no CO2 from blood).

Graphical Representation:

  • Point E corresponds to infinite V/Q, with very high PO2 and almost zero PCO2.
  • Other points on the curve:
    • Point A: V/Q = 0 (shunt, airway obstruction) → low PO2 (~40), high PCO2 (~46).
    • Point C: Normal alveoli (V/Q = 0.8) → PO2 ~100, PCO2 ~40.

Key Concept:

  • Pulmonary embolism → alveolar dead space → V/Q = ∞ → Point E.
  • Airway obstruction → shunt → V/Q = 0 → Point A.

question_text: A 28-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with multiple fractures suffered in a car accident. Arterial blood gases are ordered while the patient is breathing room air. After obtaining the arterial blood sample, the blood-gas technician draws room air into the syringe before measuring the blood-gas values. As a result, which of the following is true?
option_a: The measured values of both PaO2 and PaCO2 will be higher than the patient's actual values
option_b: The measured values of both PaO2 and PaCO2 will be lower than the patient's actual values
option_c: The measured PaO2 will be higher and the measured PaCO2 will be lower than the patient's actual blood gas values
option_d: The measured PaO2 will be lower and the measured PaCO2 will be higher than the patient's actual blood gas values
explanation:
Room air contains 21% O2 and 0.04% CO2, yielding a PIo2 of 160 mmHg and a PICO2 of 0.3 mmHg.

Thus, if a sample of arterial blood is equilibrated with room air, the measured Pao2 will have an inaccurately high reading and the Paco2 will have an inaccurately low reading.

For this reason, collecting an "anaerobic" blood sample is critical in blood gas analysis. Also, once the sample is obtained, the syringe should be placed in a container of crushed ice to prevent any metabolism by the red blood cells, which can also affect the accuracy of the readings.

In addition to being certain that an air bubble is not left in the syringe, it is best to use a glass rather than a plastic syringe because the arterial pressure will pump the blood sample into a glass syringe without requiring aspiration, and glass is more impermeable to the diffusion of gases than plastic.

A plastic syringe is permissible if one is drawing the blood sample from an arterial line rather than doing an arterial "stick" and if the sample is promptly analyzed.

question_text: As we know that fetal Hb is different from the HbA. Why Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) having more affinity with O2 than Adult hemoglobin (HbA). Which of these is main reson for that?
explanation:
• Fetal Hemoglobin (HbF) vs. Adult Hemoglobin (HbA):
    • HbF has a higher affinity for oxygen compared to HbA, which is crucial for the fetus to effectively extract oxygen from maternal blood in the placenta.

Main Reason for Increased Affinity of HbF

  • Lower Levels of 2,3-DPG:
    • HbF binds less effectively to 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) than HbA, leading to a left shift in the O2-Hb dissociation curve.
    • This left shift indicates that HbF holds onto oxygen more tightly, enhancing its oxygen-binding capacity.

Mechanism

  • γ Chains vs. β Chains:
    • The γ chains in HbF have less avidity for 2,3-DPG compared to the β chains in HbA.
    • As a result, HbF maintains a higher affinity for oxygen allowing for efficient oxygen transfer from the mother to the fetus a phenomenon known as the Double Bohr Effect.

Effects of Other Factors

  • O2, CO2, H+:
    • While changes in O2, CO2, and H+ concentrations can affect the affinity of both HbF and HbA, these factors influence them equally. The unique structure of HbF regarding 2,3-DPG is the main reason for its increased affinity.

Why Not Others

  • Option A (O2): Incorrect; while oxygen levels affect affinity, they do not explain the inherent difference between HbF and HbA.
  • Option B (CO2): Incorrect; CO2 levels similarly influence both types of hemoglobin, but do not account for the unique properties of HbF.
  • Option C (H+): Incorrect; hydrogen ion concentration impacts oxygen affinity, but again does not distinguish between HbF and HbA.

Key Takeaways

  • Correct answer: Option D, 2, 3 DPG.
  • Fetal hemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen due to lower levels of 2,3-DPG, enhancing oxygen extraction from maternal blood.

question_text: Oxygen-hemoglobin (Oxy-Hb) equilibrium curve (dissociation or association curve) explains the relationship between partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) in blood with oxygen saturation of Hb. Here in this phenomenon binding of O2 with HB is______?
explanation:
• Binding Mechanism:
    • Hemoglobin (Hb) is a protein with four subunits, each containing a heme group that binds oxygen (O2).
    • Each heme group has one iron (Fe2+) atom, which is crucial for oxygen binding.
  • Nature of Binding:
    • The process of binding O2 to hemoglobin involves a reversible reaction where oxygen molecules attach to the iron in the heme without altering the chemical structure of hemoglobin.
    • This binding is termed a physical process (or physiochemical) because it does not involve the formation of new chemical bonds or the transformation of substances; rather, it is a non-covalent interaction.
  • Oxygenation vs. Oxidation:
    • The process is referred to as oxygenation (binding of O2) rather than oxidation (which involves the transfer of electrons and changes in oxidation state), meaning the iron remains in the ferrous state (Fe2+) while bound to oxygen.

Why Not Others

  • Option A: Chemical binding - Incorrect; the process does not involve new chemical bonds being formed.
  • Option C: A+B - Incorrect; only the physical binding is applicable here.
  • Option D: Neither A nor B - Incorrect; physical binding is the correct description of how oxygen attaches to hemoglobin.

Key Takeaways:

  • Correct answer: Option B, Physical binding.
  • The binding of oxygen to hemoglobin is a reversible physical process, not a chemical one, characterized by non-covalent interactions that maintain hemoglobin's structure during oxygen transport.

• Right Shift of O2-Hb Dissociation Curve:
    • Indicates a decreased affinity of hemoglobin (Hb) for oxygen (O2), meaning that hemoglobin releases oxygen more readily to the tissues.

Factors Causing Right Shift

    • Conditions with low oxygen availability can lead to adaptations that enhance oxygen release, contributing to a right shift.
  • Hypercapnia:

  • Fever:
    • Elevated body temperature increases metabolic activity, leading to a right shift and improved oxygen delivery to tissues.
  • Increased 2,3-DPG:
    • Elevated levels of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) enhance the ability of hemoglobin to release oxygen, especially in chronic hypoxic conditions and under certain hormonal influences (like growth hormone and thyroid hormones).

question_text:
List the factor(s) from following cause left shift of O2-Hb dissociation curve.
1) Hypoxia
2) Hypercapnia
3) Alkalosis
4) Fever

explanation:
• Left Shift of O2-Hb Dissociation Curve:
    • Indicates an increased affinity of hemoglobin (Hb) for oxygen (O2), meaning that hemoglobin holds onto oxygen more tightly and releases less to the tissues.
    • This physiological response is beneficial in certain conditions, such as fetal development, where it allows fetal hemoglobin to effectively extract oxygen from maternal blood.

Factors Causing Left Shift

  • Decreased H+ Ion Concentration (Increased pH):
    • A higher pH (alkalosis) reduces H+ ion concentration, leading to a left shift and enhancing Hb's affinity for O2.
  • Decreased PCO2:
    • Lower levels of carbon dioxide lead to a decrease in acidity, contributing to increased oxygen affinity.
  • Decreased 2,3-DPG:
    • Lower levels of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), often seen in stored blood, also lead to a left shift as 2,3-DPG normally decreases Hb's affinity for O2.
  • Decreased Body Temperature:
    • Hypothermia can cause a left shift, as lower temperatures increase O2 affinity.
  • Fetal Hemoglobin:
    • Fetal Hb has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult Hb, leading to a left shift.
  • Myoglobin:
    • Myoglobin, which stores oxygen in muscle tissues, also has a higher affinity for O2 compared to hemoglobin.
  • Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning:
    • CO binds tightly to hemoglobin, preventing oxygen release and mimicking a left shift.

Why Not Others

  • Option A (1, 2, and 3): Incorrect; while alkalosis contributes to a left shift, hypoxia and hypercapnia actually lead to a right shift.
  • Option B (2, 3, 4, and 5): Incorrect; this option includes hypercapnia, which causes a right shift, and omits important factors like fetal hemoglobin and myoglobin.
  • Option C (2 and 3): Incorrect; hypercapnia is not associated with a left shift, as it decreases pH and increases acidity.

Key Takeaways:

  • The left shift of the O2-Hb dissociation curve signifies increased oxygen affinity, leading to less oxygen available for tissues and is primarily caused by alkalosis.

question_text: In which of the following processes, surface tension in alveoli is increased?
option_d: Goes from standing to supine position
explanation:
Explanation:

Surface tension in alveoli is governed by the Law of Laplace (P = 2T/r) and the effect of pulmonary surfactant.

  • Alveolar surface tension is determined by the fluid lining the alveoli and the effect of surfactant secreted by type II alveolar cells.
  • During inspiration, alveoli expand and surfactant molecules become more spread out, lowering their concentration at the air-liquid interface.
  • This reduced effectiveness of surfactant leads to a relative increase in surface tension.
  • Conversely, during expiration, alveoli shrink, surfactant molecules are more concentrated, and surface tension decreases, preventing alveolar collapse.(Option B ruled out)

Explanation of other options:

Stands from supine position (Option C): This affects lung volumes and perfusion distribution but not directly alveolar surface tension.

Goes from standing to supine position (Option D): Alters functional residual capacity and ventilation-perfusion matching, not surface tension directly.

Key Takeaway:

Law of Laplace Formula: Pressure (P) = 2 × Surface Tension (T) ÷ Radius (r).

  • Implication: The smaller the radius of the alveolus, the greater the pressure needed to keep it open.
  • Without surfactant, Small alveoli would collapse into larger alveoli (atelectasis) due to higher collapsing pressure.
  • With surfactant: Surface tension is reduced more in smaller alveoli (higher surfactant concentration as alveoli shrink), equalising pressures between small and large alveoli → stabilises alveoli.
  • Clinical relevance: In premature infants with surfactant deficiency, alveoli tend to collapse (Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome) because Laplace's law acts unopposed.

question_text: A 68-year-old woman with pulmonary fibrosis, who presents with a complaint of increasing dyspnea while performing activities of daily living, is referred for pulmonary function testing. Which of the following laboratory values is consistent with her diagnosis?
option_a: Decreased diffusing capacity of the lung
explanation:
In pulmonary fibrosis, the diffusing capacity of the lung is decreased due to an increase in the thickness of the diffusional barrier, as predicted by Fick's law of diffusion.

Pulmonary fibrosis causes "stiff" lungs, and is characterized by a decrease in lung compliance and an increase in lung elastic recoil.

This results in pulmonary function findings typical of a restrictive impairment, including a decrease in all lung volumes and capacities and a ratio of the forced expiratory volume exhaled in one second (FEV1.0) to the total forced vital capacity (FVC) that is normal or increased.

Although airway resistance is increased at lower lung volumes, the airway resistance in restrictive disorders is normal when corrected for lung volume.

An increased airway resistance is the hallmark of an obstructive impairment.

question_text:
A 150-lb patient scheduled for abdominal surgery is sent for pre-op evaluation and testing. His chest x-ray is normal, and pulmonary function results on room air show:
Tidal volume = 600 mL
Respiratory rate = 12/min
Vital capacity = 5000 mL
PaO2 = 90 mmHg
PaCO2 = 40 mmHg
PECO2 = 28 mmHg
The volume of the patient's physiological dead space, determined by applying Bohr's equation, equals which of the following?
explanation:
Physiological deadspace is the volume of the respiratory tract, that is ventilated but not perfused by the pulmonary circulation. Bohr's equation for determination of the ratio of the physiologic deadspace (VD) to the tidal volume (VT) is

VD/VT = PaCO2 - PECO2/PaCO2

VD/VT = 40 - 28/40 = 0.3

VD/VT x VT = VD

0.3 x 600 mL = 180 mL

Physiologic Deadspace Volume = Anatomic + Alveolar Deadspace Anatomic deadspace can be measured by Fowler's technique, but is often estimated as 1 mL per pound of body weight. Because there is normally no alveolar deadspace, physiologic deadspace volume approximates anatomic deadspace volume in persons with normal lung function.

Reference: Ganong, pp 658-660. Levitzky, pp 67-71.

question_text: A healthy, 24-year-old man is prescribed sustained-release bupropion (Zyban) for smoking cessation. question_text: A 72-year-old woman presents to her physician with dyspnea. Pulmonary function tests revealed an increase, rather than a decrease, in the diffusing capacity of the lung. Which of the following conditions best accounts for an increase in the diffusing capacity?
explanation:
The diffusing capacity is the volume of gas transported across the lung per minute per mm Hg partial pressure difference.

Diffusing capacity is measured by measuring the transfer of oxygen or carbon monoxide across the alveolar - capillary membrane.

Because the partial pressure of oxygen and carbon monoxide is affected by their chemical reactions with hemoglobin, as well as their transfer through the membrane, the diffusing capacity of the lung is determined both by the diffusing capacity of the membrane itself, as well as by the reaction with hemoglobin.

Increases in the diffusing capacity can be produced by increasing the concentration of hemoglobin within the blood (polycythemia).

The diffusing capacity of the membrane can be calculated by rearranging Fick's law for diffusion, and is related to the ratio of the surface area available for diffusion and the thickness of the alveolar-capillary interface.

The area available for diffusion is decreased by alveolar-septal departitioning in emphysema and by obstruction of the pulmonary vascular bed by pulmonary emboli.

The thickness of the diffusional barrier is increased by interstitial fibrosis and by interstitial or alveolar edema found in congestive heart failure.

Reference: Ganong, pp 660-661. Kasper et al., pp 201-204. Levitzky, pp 130-140.

question_text: A 49-year-old coal miner presents with dyspnea, a nonproductive cough, and decreased exercise tolerance. explanation:

Patients with restrictive lung disease have small tidal volumes.

The diffusing capacity will be reduced because the small lung volumes reduce the surface area available for gas exchange, and the fibrotic changes in the lungs increase the thickness of the diffusion barrier.

The presence of V/Q abnormalities is indicated by the need for supplemental oxygen.

Reference: Levitzky, pp 41-46. Stead, pp 255-257.

question_text: A spirometer can be used to measure directly which of the following?
explanation:
A spirometer is an instrument that records the volume of air moved into and out of the lungs during breathing, and therefore can only be used to measure lung volumes and capacities that can be exchanged with the environment.

Spirometry can be used to measure the inspiratory capacity, which is the maximal amount of gas that can be inspired following a tidal expiration.

Spirometry cannot be used to meaure the volume of the gas that remains in the lungs following a maximal expiration, that is, the residual volume, and thus cannot directly measure the lung capacities that contain the residual volume, that is, the functional residual capacity and the total lung capacity.

Every lung volume and capacity, including the residual volume, contains deadspace volume, and thus spirometry cannot be used to measure the physiological dead space.

question_text: A 51-year-old male presents with shortness of breath after climbing stairs. Patient has chronic cough. His respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Pulmonary function tests show decreased forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and reduced FEV1/FVC ratio. What is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
• COPD is a chronic, progressive lung disease commonly caused by smoking, characterized by persistent airflow limitation. COPD is characterized by airway obstruction, resulting in decreased FEV1 and a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio. It often presents with chronic shortness of breath and may be linked to a history of smoking.
  • Asthma is a chronic inflammatory condition of the airways characterized by intermittent airflow obstruction. Asthma: While asthma also causes decreased FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio, it is usually reversible and often linked to wheezing and specific triggers.
  • Pulmonary fibrosis is a form of restrictive lung disease that leads to scarring and stiffening of the lung tissue. Pulmonary fibrosis: Causes restrictive lung disease and typically shows a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio.
  • A pulmonary embolism (PE) is a blockage of one of the pulmonary arteries due to a blood clot. Pulmonary embolism: Causes sudden onset shortness of breath with normal pulmonary function tests.

Why Not Other Options:

  • A. Asthma: Often reversible and presents with wheezing, unlike COPD.
  • B. Pulmonary fibrosis: Results in a restrictive pattern, not an obstructive pattern as seen in COPD.
  • D. Pulmonary embolism: Sudden onset, with normal PFT results, unlike COPD's chronic progression.

Key Takeaways:

  • COPD is characterized by decreased FEV1 and reduced FEV1/FVC ratio due to airway obstruction.
  • Asthma is reversible, and pulmonary fibrosis and embolism present differently.

question_text:

• Pulmonary fibrosis (Correct): The CT scan reveals honeycombing, a hallmark of pulmonary fibrosis. This pattern signifies significant fibrosis and remodelling of the lung parenchyma, commonly seen in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)/Usual interstitial pneumonitis(UIP). leading to progressive dyspnea.

  • Bronchiectasis: This condition is associated with dilated bronchi and thickened airway walls, which do not present with honeycombing on CT. It shows tram track appearance on Xray and CT.

Key Takeaways:

question_text: A patient with emphysema is referred for his annual pulmonary function testing to assess the progression of his disease. As a result of alveolarseptal departitioning in emphysema, there is a decrease in which of the following?
explanation:
Destruction of the alveolar septa in emphysema causes a loss of pulmonary capillaries, which decreases the surface area available for diffusion, and therefore decreases the rate of diffusion in accordance with Fick's law.

Alveolar septal departitioning with destruction of pulmonary capillaries results in enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles and an increase in alveolar deadspace, that is, alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused.

Elastic fibers are also found in the alveolar septa. In emphysema, the destruction of elastic fibers decreases lung elastic recoil, and increases lung compliance.

The loss of elastic recoil increases intrapleural pressures, which decreases transmural pressure across the noncartilaginous airways (less radial traction), which decreases airway caliber and increases airway resistance in accordance with Poiseuille's law.

In addition, the loss of elastic recoil impairs the ability to oppose dynamic compression of the airways.

As a result, dynamic compression occurs closer to the alveoli during forced expirations, resulting in air trapping and an increase in residual volume and total lung capacity.

Reference: Ganong, pp 654-655, 660-661, 689. Levitzky, pp 22-23, 39-40, 58-59, 81, 140.

question_text: A sedentary individual goes to her physician's office for a cardiopulmonary exercise stress test evaluation prior to starting a weight-loss exercise regimen. Physiological changes that occur during deep inspirations as lung volume approaches total lung capacity include which of the following?
option_a: Elastic recoil of the lungs decreases
explanation:
Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) varies with lung volume. PVR is lowest at functional residual capacity, and increases at both high and low lung volumes. The increased pulmonary vascular resistance seen at total lung capacity (TLC) is due to an increase in the resistance of the alveolar vessels (pulmonary capillaries) caused by compression by the high alveolar volume.

The increased pulmonary vascular resistance seen at residual volume is due to an increase in the resistance of the extra-alveolar vessels caused by compression by the positive intrapleural pressure generated during a forced expiration.

As lung volume increases toward TLC, the compliance of the lungs (slope of pressure-volume curve) decreases and elastic recoil of the lung increases, that is, the lungs resist further expansion. Intrapleural pressure becomes more subatmospheric during inspiration, approaching -30 cm H2O at TLC; as a result, the transmural pressure across the intrathoracic airways (Pin - Pout) increases, which increases airway radius, and decreases airway resistance according to Poiseuille's law.

question_text: Which one of the following is related to the release of bicarbonate in exchange for chloride in the RBC?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Chloride Shift (Hamburger phenomenon) is the exchange of bicarbonate (HCO3-) and chloride (Cl-) ions between RBCs and plasma to maintain electrical neutrality.

CO2+H2O⇌H2CO3⇌H++HCO3-

  • CO2 enters RBCs and reacts with water (H2O) via carbonic anhydrase to form H2CO3 (carbonic acid), which then dissociates into HCO3- (bicarbonate) and H+ (proton).
  • 3- exits the RBC into the plasma, and to maintain electrical neutrality, Cl- enters the RBC (this is the chloride shift).

Explanation of Other Options:

Bohr's effect (Option A)

The Bohr effect describes how increased CO2 and decreased pH lead to a rightward shift in the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, meaning haemoglobin releases more oxygen to tissues. It is related to oxygen unloading in tissues but not directly related to bicarbonate exchange in RBCs.

Haldane effect (Option B)

The Haldane effect describes how deoxygenated hemoglobin binds more CO2 and H+ ions, enhancing CO2 transport in venous blood.

This effect facilitates CO2 loading in tissues and CO2 unloading in the lungs.

None of the above (Option C)

Since Chloride Shift (option C) is correct, this option is incorrect.

Key Takeaways:

The chloride shift involves the exchange of bicarbonate (3-) and chloride (Cl-) ions between RBCs and plasma, helping to maintain electrical neutrality. The Bohr effect relates to oxygen unloading, not bicarbonate exchange. The Haldane effect involves CO2 and H+ ion binding to deoxygenated haemoglobin, aiding CO2 transport. The chloride shift is essential in the transport of CO2 in the blood and is a key physiological process.

question_text: A 24-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset chest pain and shortness of breath after a long flight. She has a respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute, and ABG shows PaO2 of 70 mmHg, PaCO2 of 30 mmHg, and pH of 7.48. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Pulmonary embolism (Correct): The patient's history of a long flight suggests venous stasis, which increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis leading to a pulmonary embolism. The ABG shows respiratory alkalosis (high pH, low PaCO2) due to hyperventilation, a common response to hypoxia caused by the embolism.
  • Pleural effusion: Typically presents with gradual onset of breathlessness and does not commonly show hyperventilation or respiratory alkalosis like pulmonary embolism.
  • Pneumothorax: While it can cause sudden chest pain and dyspnea, ABG findings are more variable. It often presents with decreased breath sounds and may not consistently show hyperventilation.
  • Acute asthma exacerbation: Usually presents with wheezing and respiratory distress but is less likely to occur after prolonged immobility. It often results in hypoxemia and CO2 retention rather than hyperventilation.

Option B: The most likely diagnosis is Pulmonary embolism. The patient has several key risk factors for PE, including a long flight (immobility), and presents with typical symptoms of sudden-onset chest pain and dyspnea. The ABG findings of hypoxemia, hypocapnia, and respiratory alkalosis are also classic for PE, making it the most probable diagnosis in this scenario.

Why Not Other Options:

  • A. Pleural effusion: Gradual onset, no hyperventilation or respiratory alkalosis.
  • C. Pneumothorax: Variable ABG findings; sudden decrease in oxygenation is characteristic but not consistent with hyperventilation.
  • D. Acute asthma exacerbation: Presents with wheezing; typically associated with hypoxemia and CO2 retention.

Key Takeaways:

  • Pulmonary embolism is suggested by sudden chest pain and shortness of breath after prolonged immobility, with ABG findings showing respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation.
  • Other conditions have distinct presentations and ABG profiles that differentiate them from pulmonary embolism.

question_text: A 22-year-old college student flies to Leh, which is at an altitude of 3700 m above sea level. She experiences nausea, headache, mental confusion, and blurred vision. Which of the following is the underlying mechanism for these findings?
option_a: Increase in sympathetic activity leading to vasoconstriction of cerebral vessels, leading to transudation of fluid
option_b: Decrease in PaO<sub>2</sub> leading to vasoconstriction of cerebral vessels, leading to transudation of fluid
option_c: Decrease in PaO<sub>2</sub> leading to vasodilatation of cerebral vessels, leading to transudation of fluid
option_d: Decrease in pH leading to vasodilatation of cerebral vessels, leading to transudation of fluid
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's symptoms are characteristic of Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS), progressing towards High-Altitude Cerebral Edema (HACE). The pathophysiology is a cascade of events initiated by hypobaric hypoxia.

Pathophysiological Cascade of High-Altitude Cerebral Edema (HACE):

  • Initial Event (Hypoxemia): At high altitude, low atmospheric pressure reduces the partial pressure of oxygen. This leads to systemic hypoxemia (decreased PaO2).
  • Cerebral Response (Vasodilation): This severe hypoxemia is a potent stimulus for cerebral vasodilation. The brain attempts to increase blood flow to compensate for the low oxygen content.
  • Pathological Consequence (Edema): The vasodilation increases capillary hydrostatic pressure, disrupting the blood-brain barrier and causing vasogenic edema (fluid transudation) into the brain tissue.
  • Clinical Manifestation: This edema increases intracranial pressure, leading to the patient's neurological symptoms of headache, confusion, and nausea.

Key Takeaway:

  • Altitude Illnesses: Rapid ascent can cause a spectrum of illnesses, including:
    • Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS): A milder form with headache, nausea, and fatigue. It develops within 6-24 hours of ascent above 2,500 m
    • High-Altitude Cerebral Edema (HACE): A severe, life-threatening progression of AMS.
    • High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema (HAPE): Life-threatening fluid accumulation in the lungs. It develops within 2-4 days o f altitude ascending.
  • Pathophysiology of HACE: The core mechanism is hypoxemia-induced cerebral vasodilation, leading to vasogenic edema and increased intracranial pressure.
  • Contrasting Effects of Hypoxia:
    • Brain: Hypoxia → Vasodilation → Increased blood flow → Cerebral Edema (HACE)
    • Lungs: Hypoxia → Vasoconstriction (Hypoxic Pulmonary Vasoconstriction) → Pulmonary Hypertension → Pulmonary Edema (HAPE)

question_text: A person who recently moved to a high-altitude environment develops hypoxia. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

At high altitudes, atmospheric pressure falls, resulting in a lower partial pressure of inspired oxygen (PO2). This directly decreases alveolar and subsequently arterial PO2, leading to hypoxic hypoxia, the most common type encountered in such situations.

Types of hypoxia:

  • Hypoxic hypoxia: ↓ arterial PO2 (e.g., high altitude, hypoventilation, diffusion defects, V/Q mismatch).
  • Anemic hypoxia: Normal PO2 but ↓ oxygen-carrying capacity due to low Hb.
  • Stagnant hypoxia: Inadequate blood flow (e.g., heart failure, shock).
  • Histotoxic hypoxia: Cells unable to utilize oxygen (e.g., cyanide poisoning).

Impact at high altitude:

  • ↓ Partial pressure of oxygen → ↓ Hemoglobin saturation (SaO2) → ↓ Oxygen delivery to tissues.
  • Both dissolved and Hb-bound oxygen fall, causing tissue hypoxia.

Explanation of other options:

Reduced hemoglobin concentration (Option A): Causes anemic hypoxia, but at high altitude, hemoglobin levels are normal initially. Not the primary mechanism here.

Reduced blood lactate concentration (Option C): Irrelevant in this context. In fact, hypoxia increases lactate production due to anaerobic metabolism, not decreases it.

Increased partial pressure of carbon dioxide (Option D): Leads to hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis, which can worsen hypoxia, but high-altitude hypoxia is primarily due to low PO2, not CO2 retention.

  • Cardiovascular: Sympathetic activation → ↑ heart rate and cardiac output; systemic hypoxia → vasodilation to improve tissue perfusion.
  • Tissue/Muscle: Chronic hypoxia → mitochondrial biogenesis, capillary density up, ↑ myoglobin; local factors promote angiogenesis.

Increased mitochondria (Option C): Muscle adapts with more mitochondria and capillaries to enhance oxidative metabolism under hypoxia.

question_text: A group of third year medical students accompanied a medical mission team to Peru. After arriving at the airport in Bolivia, they hiked to a remote mountain village in the Andes. At this elevation of 18,000 ft, the barometric pressure was 380 mmHg, resulting in a PO2 of the dry inspired air of what?
explanation:
According to Dalton's Law, the partial pressure of a gas is the product of the fractional composition of the gas and the total pressure of the gaseous mixture. Oxygen constitutes approximately 21% of dry atmospheric air.

Therefore, the partial pressure of O2 in dry atmospheric air equals the fractional concentration of oxygen (FIO2) times the atmospheric (barometric) pressure. At sea level, the barometric pressure is 760 mmHg, yielding a PIO2 of 160mmHg. At high altitude, the barometric pressure decreases in proportion to the decreased weight of the air above it.

At an elevation of 18,000 feet in the Peruvian Andes, the barometric pressure is 380 mmHg, yielding a PIO2 of 80 mmHg. Once inside the respiratory tract, the inspired air becomes warmed and humidified. The partial pressure of H2O vapor is temperature-, rather than concentration- dependent, and at body temperature (37ºC) is 47 mmHg.

The presence of H2O vapor reduces the partial pressure of the other gases in the atmosphere, and the PH2O must be subtracted from the total barometric pressure before multiplying by the fractional concentration of a gas to yield the partial pressure of the gas.

Thus, at sea level, the humidified PIo2 in the conducting airways is 0.21 (760-47) or 150 mmHg, whereas, at 18,000 feet, the humidified, tracheal Po2 would be 0.21 (380-47) or 70 mmHg.

Reference: Ganong, pp 647-648. Levitzky, pp 71-72.

question_text: If there is no net transudation across a capillary with a capillary hydrostatic pressure of 18 mm Hg, capillary oncotic pressure of 27 mm Hg, and interstitial oncotic pressure of 7 mm Hg, what should be the interstitial hydrostatic pressure?
explanation:
Explanation:

The movement of fluid across a capillary is governed by Starling forces. For there to be "no net transudation," the forces favoring filtration must be perfectly balanced by the forces favoring reabsorption, meaning the Net Filtration Pressure (NFP) is zero.

The Starling equation is:

NFP = (Forces Out) - (Forces In) = (Pc + πi) - (Pi + πc)

Where:

  • Pc = Capillary hydrostatic pressure
  • πi = Interstitial oncotic pressure
  • Pi = Interstitial hydrostatic pressure
  • πc = Capillary oncotic pressure

Setting NFP to 0 and substituting the given values:
0 = (18 + 7) - (Pi + 27)

0 = 25 - (Pi + 27)

Pi + 27 = 25

Pi = 25 - 27

Pi = -2 mm Hg

A slightly negative interstitial hydrostatic pressure is normal and is thought to be generated by the continuous pumping action of the lymphatic system.

question_text: A gentelman is hyperventilating in one morning. Based on your knowledege of respiratory medicine which of these is true due to hyperventilation?
option_a: P50 & Hb affinity for O2 increases
option_b: P50 & Hb affinity for O2 decreases
option_c: P50 decreases, Hb affinity for O2 increases
option_d: P50 increases, Hb affinity for O2 decreases
explanation:
• Hyperventilation Effects:
    • Hyperventilation is characterized by increased respiratory rate, leading to excessive elimination of CO2.
    • This results in decreased PCO2 (partial pressure of carbon dioxide) and increased PO2 (partial pressure of oxygen) in the blood.
  • P50:
    • The P50 value is the partial pressure of oxygen at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated.
    • A normal P50 is approximately 25 mm Hg.
    • A decrease in P50 indicates an increase in hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, allowing for better oxygen uptake at lower pressures.
  • Bohr Effect:
    • The Bohr effect describes how changes in CO2 and pH affect hemoglobin's oxygen-binding affinity.
    • With lower CO2 levels from hyperventilation, the blood becomes more alkaline (higher pH), which increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.

Why Not Others

  • Option A: P50 & Hb affinity for O2 increases - Incorrect; hyperventilation causes a drop in PCO2, leading to increased affinity, not both increasing.
  • Option B: P50 & Hb affinity for O2 decreases - Incorrect; while P50 decreases, hemoglobin's affinity increases due to lower CO2.
  • Option D: P50 increases, Hb affinity for O2 decreases - Incorrect; during hyperventilation, P50 decreases, resulting in increased affinity for oxygen.

Key Takeaways

  • Correct answer: Option C, P50 decreases, Hb affinity for O2 increases.
  • Hyperventilation leads to reduced PCO2 and increased PO2, resulting in a decreased P50 and an increased affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, enhancing oxygen uptake efficiency in the lungs.

question_text: A 68-year-old male with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease entered the Emergency Department complaining of shortness of breath. His respirations were 35 per minute and labored. He had a productive cough and rales were heard over all lung fields. The patient had a rather ashen complexion and his nail beds gave clear evidence of cyanosis. An arterial blood sample was obtained and a chest x-ray was ordered. The patient was then placed on an O2 mask delivering 40% O2. One-half hour later, the physician was called to the bedside by the nurse who found the patient unresponsive. The patient's complexion had changed to a flushed pink with no trace of cyanosis. His respirations were quiet at a rate of 6 per minute and a tidal volume of 300 mL. Repeat arterial blood gases showed that his arterial PCO2 had increased from 55 to 70 mmHg, and his PaO2 increased from 55 to 70 mmHg. Oxygen therapy most likely resulted in which of the following?
option_c: Increased firing of carotid body chemoreceptors
explanation:
The hypercapnic drive for breathing is attenuated in COPD patients with chronic hypercapnia because compensated respiratory acidosis in the cerebrospinal fluid eliminates the direct stimulus to the central chemoreceptors.

Because alveolar ventilation also causes hypoxemia, the decrease in PaO2 stimulating the peripheral chemoreceptors (hypoxic drive) becomes the primary drive to breathe in chronic hypercapnia.

Administration of too much oxygen can raise PaO2 above the threshold necessary for adequate firing of the peripheral chemoreceptors, which will "knock out" the hypoxic drive and cause an O2-induced hypoventilation, as evidenced by a further rise in PaCO2.

The potential for O2-induced hypoventilation should not be a deterrent to oxygen therapy when indicated in patients with COPD, as supplemental oxygen is the only therapy for COPD shown to extend life, in addition to improving IQ, exercise tolerance, and cor pulmonale.

The central chemoreceptors respond to changes in [H+] in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which are brought about by changes in arterial PCO2. The failure of CO2 to increase ventilation indicates that the central chemoreceptors are not functioning properly.

The peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated by hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidemia, and thus are functioning appropriately because ventilation decreased when PO2 was increased (hyperoxia).

Obstructive sleep apnea is caused by upper airway obstruction due to hypotonic pharyngeal or genioglossus muscles or too much fat around the pharynx, but not because of obstruction of the tracheobronchial tree by bronchospasm.

Diaphragmatic fatigue can cause hypoventilation, but is not associated with apneic episodes, perhaps because of the increased contribution of the accessory muscles of respiration.

The reflex effect of stimulation of the irritant receptors by mechanical or chemical irritation of the airways is bronchoconstriction and cough.

Reference: Ganong, pp 672-678, 693-694. Levitzky, pp 196-198, 201-210.

A 47-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by paramedics. She was found unconscious on a park bench by a bystander. Her history is unobtainable.
Vitals include a pulse of 64/min, a respiratory rate of 7/min, and a blood pressure of 90/70 mm Hg. On examination, the patient is unresponsive to voice and touch but shows a flexor response to pain. Her breathing is shallow. The pupils are constricted, and a response to light cannot be determined.
An arterial blood gas sample reveals:
pH - 7.26
PCO2 - 70 mmHg
HCO3 - 26mEq/L
explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with an opioid overdose and shows the typical triad of coma, respiratory depression, and miosis.

Furthermore, the arterial blood gas analysis shows a respiratory acidosis, which is expected due to decreased ventilation that results in carbon dioxide retention (elevated arterial Pco,) and decreased pH. Renal compensation then increases HCO, but this develops slowly, over at least 24 hours, and often the acute respiratory insult has resolved by then.

Opioids act directly on the respiratory center and can cause significant depression in overdose states. Another potential cause of acute respiratory acidosis is sudden airway obstruction which would trap exhaled air, including carbon dioxide, in the lungs. The graph below illustrates the ABG changes seen in respiratory acidosis and alkalosis.

Option A: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients retain CO, over a prolonged period, and thus renal compensation (increased serum bicarbonate) compensates for the pulmonary acidosis. This patient, however, has an uncompensated respiratory acidosis more in line with an acute event (opioid overdose) than a chronic condition. Furthermore, an acute exacerbation of COPD would likely not render a person unconscious unless exceptionally severe.

Option B: Type 1 diabetics dependent upon insulin can develop diabetic ketoacidosis following non-compliance with medications and diet, infection, pregnancy, myocardial infarction, pancreatitis, and others. Diabetic ketoacidosis is a type of metabolic acidosis which would present with a decreased blood bicarbonate level and decreased carbon dioxide due to increased ventilation, which will blow off increasing quantities of the gas.

Option C: Most diuretics, like furosemide and thiazides, cause potassium and hydrogen ion wasting, leading to a contraction alkalosis. Since this patient presented with acidosis, diuretic abuse is unlikely.

Learning objective: Respiratory acidosis is characterized by an increased PCO2 and lowered pH. After compensation develops, the HCO3- concentration increases. Opioids are a known cause of respiratory depression that can cause respiratory acidosis.

Reference: Guyton & Hall, 14th edition pg no. 560, 561, 562
